..(Wednesday night through Monday)
Issued at 455 AM EDT TUE SEP 29 2026

The extended portion of the forecast looks to be on track with 
the idea of a southwesterly flow pattern aloft over Kentucky
through the end of the week. This then becomes more zonal over 
the weekend with energy arriving from the northern stream 
accompanying a large trough swinging through the Great Lakes just 
in time for the new week. As a result, much higher chances for 
rain will be the rule over the weekend compared to the better part
of this current week along with the possibility of a few
thunderstorms capable of producing heavy or excessive rains.

The previous long term discussion follows:

The long-term period opens Wednesday morning with upper level 
ridging in place over the Southeast CONUS, mirrored at the surface 
by high pressure offset to the east over the Western Atlantic. This 
will be maintaining a mild southerly flow across the Ohio Valley. 
Looking upstream, a mean 500 hPa trough will be in place over 
western Canada while a closed ~568 dam low spins over the Lower 
Colorado River Valley. The trough will be supporting an ~991 mb 
surface low over the Upper Mackenzie River Valley with a  cold front 
extending southward into the Northern High Plains and then westward 
across the Columbia River Basin. Another ~1000 mb low is noted over 
the Southern Rockies ahead of the aforementioned closed low. 

For the first few days of the long-term, the upper level ridging 
will drift eastward to off the Southeast Coast. This will keep 
southerly flow and an unseasonably warm air mass (mean 850 hPa 
temperatures ~16-18C, as per the LREF) and mostly dry conditions in 
place over eastern Kentucky through Friday. In the meantime, the 
closed low over the Desert Southwest will open up and be captured 
the eastward-propagating northern-stream trough. As that trough 
shifts eastward, it will suppress the 500 hPa ridging over the Ohio 
Valley, transitioning the flow aloft to quasi-zonal/weakly troughed. 
The cold front associated with the trough will move into the Ohio 
Valley but then struggle to make further southeastward progress 
Friday night-Saturday night as energy ejects out of the opening low 
and rides along the boundary. Meanwhile, PWATs could exceed the 90th 
percentile if the NAEFS/ECMWF mean solution materializes, amidst 
deep moisture advection from the Gulf of America. If ingredients 
come together ideally, a decent soaking rainfall is possible across 
portions of eastern Kentucky or adjacent regions this weekend, but 
forecaster confidence is low. From a more sensible standpoint, this 
pattern will bring back the return of a summer-like feel for the 
remainder of the work week with dew points recovering back through 
the 50s and into the 60s while afternoon temperatures peak in the 
low to mid 80s from Wednesday through Friday. Some of the hotter 
portions of the Cumberland could flirt with the upper 80s. Rain 
chances will then knock back the high temperatures for Saturday but 
it will still be quite humid with the threat of rainfall and 
possibly a few rumbles of thunder.  

Change will be around the corner to close out the first weekend of 
October. Within the broad upper level troughing, a quick-moving 
shortwave trough transiting the 49th Parallel (US-Canada border) 
over the weekend will phase with northern stream energy diving 
southeast from the Yukon. This will bring height falls to the Ohio 
Valley early next week while slinging an associated cold front 
across the Coalfields Sunday into Monday. Behind that front, LREF 
mean 850 hPa temperatures drop to ~9-11C with much drier PWATs (0.6 
to 0.8 inches) by late Monday. Rain chances taper off behind the 
first cold front on Sunday and appear minimal with this second 
boundary. Instead, the more noticeable effect will be a decline in 
temperatures to more seasonable levels for Monday with highs 
returning to the mid 60s to lower 70s and cool nighttime lows in the 
40s and 50s.
